geographic_joint: Nile–Atbara corridor with overland routes toward the Red Sea and savanna
political_mechanism: Royal and ritual centers occupied a strategic junction rather than only a riverbank.
external_link: Exchange connected sub-Saharan Africa with Mediterranean and Middle Eastern worlds.
evidence: UNESCO's archaeological landscape and peer-reviewed trade-network synthesis.
limits: A strategic position does not measure customs revenue traffic volume or state control over every caravan.

geographic_joint: Middle Nile between Egypt and inner Nubia
political_mechanism: A failed Egyptian siege was followed by a disputed pact governing peace movement and reciprocal deliveries.
external_link: The Baqt sustained a diplomatic interface between Christian Nubia and successive Muslim rulers in Egypt.
evidence: Peer-reviewed reconsideration emphasizes variable reciprocal royal exchange rather than a timeless fixed tribute schedule.
limits: The pact's terms chronology and interpretation changed; enslaved people were part of the coercive exchange and are not abstracted into a trade score.

geographic_joint: Blue–White Nile confluence near routes to Kordofan Darfur the Red Sea and Ethiopia
political_mechanism: A royal administrative and religious capital concentrated a far-southern Nile crossroads.
external_link: Soba connected riverain Nubia with savanna highland and Red Sea networks.
evidence: Recent archaeology maps a roughly 275-hectare site; written and material evidence include a Muslim district and overseas glass.
limits: Site area and imported objects do not yield population trade volume or the borders of Alwa.

geographic_joint: Ethiopian highlands linked over difficult terrain to a Red Sea port
political_mechanism: Kings connected an inland capital to Adulis and presented their rule in Ge'ez and Greek.
external_link: Ivory and other African products moved outward while Mediterranean and Indian Ocean goods moved inland.
evidence: British Museum synthesis plus archaeology of Adulis and its highland connection.
limits: Imported goods and multilingual inscriptions show connection—not a complete customs ledger or exclusive royal control of exchange.
